title: The new Eve
hook: Irenaeus: the knot of Eve's disobedience was untied by Mary's obedience

segments.voice: Yesterday, ever virgin, and Mary's honest question to the angel: how shall this be done? Your line was ever virgin. Did you ask one honest question before answering? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-nine.

Two women, two conversations, far apart in the Bible. In a garden, a woman listens to the serpent, and reaches for the fruit. In a small house in Nazareth, a young woman listens to an angel, and answers: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." Early Christian writers set those two scenes side by side, like two pages held up to the light. One of them, a bishop named Irenaeus, saw a knot in the first and the same knot coming loose in the second. Today's word: the new Eve.
screen: `A GARDEN AND A SERPENT.` → `A HOUSE AND AN ANGEL.` → `TWO PAGES HELD UP TO THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the pattern Paul started. In his letters, Paul sets Jesus beside Adam and calls him the last Adam: where the first man brought death, Christ brings life. Irenaeus took that pattern one step further. If there's a new Adam, he asked, isn't there a new Eve beside him? Second, the knot. Irenaeus wrote that the knot tied by Eve's disobedience was loosened by Mary's obedience, and that what one virgin bound through unbelief, the other set free through faith. The Catechism quotes him on this, and adds his other line: that Mary, by obeying, became a cause of salvation for herself and for the whole human race. Third, why a knot. A knot isn't cut, in Irenaeus's picture. It's untied, the same way it was tied, in reverse. Eve listened to the wrong voice; Mary listens to the right one. Eve doubted the word; Mary trusts it. Eve reached; Mary receives. The second story walks back through the first, step by step, undoing it. Fourth, the name. In Genesis, Adam names his wife Eve, in the Douay-Rheims, "because she was the mother of all the living." Christians who call Mary the new Eve hear in her a second mother of the living: mother of the one who is life, and, in Catholic teaching, mother of everyone who lives in him. None of this makes Mary the savior; the Church is clear that her yes is itself a gift of her son's grace. But it makes her yes enormous. Every tangled thing, this picture suggests, can be untied the same way it was knotted: one choice at a time, in the other direction.
screen: `A NEW ADAM, A NEW EVE.` · `WHAT ONE BOUND, THE OTHER LOOSED.` · `UNTIED THE WAY IT WAS TIED.` · `MOTHER OF ALL THE LIVING.` · then, large: `BE IT DONE TO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say yes to one thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of one invitation you've been resisting. A call to return. A task you keep postponing. A kindness you know is being asked of you. Notice the knot: the reasons, the fear, the stubbornness tied around it. Then, without forcing it, see what one small yes would look like. Not the whole thing. One loosened loop. If you pray, you can borrow Mary's words: be it done to me according to thy word. The bell holds the time.
New Eve. Mary, set beside Eve by early Christian writers: where Eve's no tied the knot, Mary's yes untied it. Today's word.
Your line: the knot untied. Today, find one small knot in your life and undo one loop of it, the same way it was tied, in reverse. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics meet the new Eve in homilies on Mary, and in the Mass readings for the Immaculate Conception, where Genesis 3 is read alongside Luke 1; the Catechism teaches it at paragraph 494.

notes: Irenaeus is paraphrased, not quoted (ANF wording: 'the knot of Eve's disobedience was loosed by the obedience of Mary. For what the virgin Eve had bound fast through unbelief, this did the virgin Mary set free through faith'). Confirm and decide whether to quote ANF if a public-domain listing is approved.
'Early Christian writers set those two scenes side by side' covers Justin Martyr and Irenaeus; no count or date given. Confirm.

Paul uses 'Adam' typology (Romans 5:14; 1 Corinthians 15:45 'the last Adam'); 'new Adam' is the traditional phrase, not Paul's wording. Script now says Paul 'calls him the last Adam' (1 Cor 15:45, unquoted).
'Mother of everyone who lives in him' reflects CCC 494 and 501; confirm.
howItsDone: 'Genesis 3 is often read alongside Luke 1' refers to the Immaculate Conception readings (Gen 3:9–15, 20; Luke 1:26–38). Confirm.
Editor pass: hook no longer places Genesis 3 and Luke 1 at 'the far ends' of the Bible's story (neither is an end); review quotes Mary's question in the exact Douay wording.
Original: חַוָּה (Ḥawwah); Genesis 3:20 links the name to 'living'. No etymology asserted beyond the verse. Confirm pointing.
